questions.question: If the reality gap is just simulator inaccuracy, why not simply build a more accurate simulator and be done?
options: High-fidelity simulators cannot be stepped fast enough to collect the millions of episodes RL needs
Some unmodeled effect always survives, so robustness across a parameter range beats chasing exactness
Accurate physics engines are non-differentiable, and policy-gradient methods require differentiable dynamics
A perfectly accurate simulator would overfit the policy to one robot's exact serial-numbered hardware
questions.explanation: Motor deadband, backlash, cable drag and sensor latency are endless; every fix reveals a smaller one. Robustness over a distribution degrades gracefully when your model is slightly wrong, which exactness never does.

questions.question: You train with slip ~ Uniform[0.0, 0.3] and then evaluate the greedy policy at slip = 0.5. What is the honest expectation?
options: Near-optimal return, because 0.5 is only slightly past the upper edge of the training range
The same return as slip = 0.3, because randomization has made the policy slip-invariant
Graceful degradation, not near-optimal — 0.5 is outside the envelope DR sampled from
A hard failure, because a value function fit on one slip range is undefined outside it
questions.explanation: Domain randomization only promises coverage inside the range it sampled from. The point of the 0.5 and 0.7 columns is to show a softer decline than the fixed-slip policy's, not to claim the envelope extends.

questions.question: What goes wrong if you widen the randomization to slip ~ Uniform[0.0, 0.9]?
options: Training diverges, because a slip resampled every episode makes the transition kernel non-Markov in the observed state
The policy becomes so risk-averse that it gives up return even under nominal conditions
The policy memorizes the mean slip of the range and then acts as if every episode were drawn at that single value
Nothing — wider is always safer, it just needs more episodes
questions.explanation: Very wide randomization acts like heavy regularization: the best policy averaged over near-random dynamics is a cautious one. Match the range to measured real variability instead of to worst-case imagination.

questions.question: In privileged teacher-student training, what is the division of labor?
options: The teacher runs on the hardware and the student runs in sim, so the split is about where each policy executes rather than what it sees
The teacher is the larger network and the student is a distilled, quantized copy of it, so the same behaviour fits inside the robot's onboard compute budget
The teacher trains with ground-truth sim state; the student sees only deployable sensors and must infer those quantities from observation history
The teacher provides the reward function and the student provides the value function
questions.explanation: Privileged information like true friction or terrain height makes the teacher's problem easy to solve, and imitation then gives the student a target it can chase from proprioception alone. The split is about information, not model size or where each runs.

questions.question: Your quadruped fails on hardware. The true gap is a 30 ms actuator delay, but your DR config randomizes lighting, textures and camera hue. What is the outcome?
options: DR still helps, since any randomization widens the training distribution and a wider distribution always transfers better
DR buys nothing here — you randomized the wrong axis and must randomize or identify the delay itself
DR helps only if you also widen the visual ranges further
The failure must be a reward-shaping bug, since DR is axis-agnostic and covers unmodelled effects automatically
questions.explanation: Randomization only confers robustness along the axes you actually vary. Profiling the real platform before choosing DR parameters is what keeps the compute pointed at the real gap.

questions.question: System identification versus domain randomization — why does the 2026 recipe use both?
options: SI covers the vision pipeline and DR covers the dynamics, so running both spans every modality that can shift between the simulator and the real platform
SI removes the need for a safety shield, and DR removes the need for any real-world data at all
SI narrows the gap on measurable parameters, but its residual error is invisible to the policy — DR is what buys tolerance for that residual
SI runs before training and DR runs at deployment time, so the two act on different phases and can never conflict
questions.explanation: A well-identified sim gives you a tight, low-noise training target; what it cannot give you is robustness to the effects it failed to identify. Randomizing on top of the identified nominal covers that leftover.
